analysis.one_liner: Requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publish detailed quarterly reports on every injury claim they receive.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a floor vote: after a single Judiciary Committee hearing in February 2016, it sat in committee until the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company facing asbestos lawsuits goes bankrupt, a court-supervised trust takes over its liability and pays people sickened by asbestos. This bill would require those trusts to file quarterly public reports naming every claimant, describing their exposure history, and explaining each payment, and to share claim and payment information with any party to an asbestos lawsuit. Supporters called it transparency for trust funds; asbestos victims' groups said it hands defendant companies detailed data to challenge claims while exposing very sick people's private information.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies defending asbestos lawsuits and their liability insurers. The quarterly reports and on-request disclosures would give them a running public ledger of who is claiming what against which trust — information they could use to contest claims, argue that claimants were exposed to their own or other companies' products instead, and slow down or shrink payouts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Companies facing asbestos lawsuits and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every asbestos bankruptcy trust to file quarterly reports on the court's public docket describing each claim received, the claimant's name and exposure history, and the basis for any payment, excluding only confidential medical records and full Social Security numbers [S2][S3].

Requires trusts, on written request, to provide information about payments and demands to any party to any lawsuit concerning asbestos liability — effectively the defendant companies and insurers still fighting these cases [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos victims and their families. People filing claims are often seriously ill with mesothelioma or asbestosis; the bill would make their names and exposure histories public and give defendant companies detailed data to dispute their claims, potentially delaying or reducing compensation.

drawbacks.text: The reporting requirements would expose claimants' names and personal exposure histories on a public court docket — sensitive information for people who are often terminally ill — even though the bill carves out confidential medical records and full Social Security numbers [S2][S3].

The disclosure runs one way: trusts must hand over claim and payment data to anyone suing over asbestos liability, but the companies facing those lawsuits face no comparable obligation, so the information advantage would tilt toward defendants in ongoing cases [S2][S3].
Added paperwork and per-request costs (charged at the trust's option) could burden trust administration and slow payments to claimants, many of whom have limited time left.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real, narrower case here: these trusts handle billions of dollars, and public reporting of aggregate payout patterns could deter fraudulent or duplicate claims and reassure trust solvency. But the bill's mechanism does not mainly serve that aim. It publishes individual claimants' names and exposure histories and routes detailed claim data directly to parties suing over asbestos liability — the defendant companies — while imposing nothing on them. The costs fall on some of the sickest people in the civil justice system, and the benefit flows to the companies defending the claims. A fraud-focused transparency bill could have been written without putting individual victims' information on a public docket.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held one hearing in two years, and died when the Congress ended without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Flake introduced the bill on February 4, 2015, with Sen. John Cornyn as the other original sponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S3][S5].

The bill would have required asbestos bankruptcy trusts to file quarterly public reports on every claim — including the claimant's name and exposure history and the basis for payment — and to share claim information with any party to an asbestos-liability lawsuit [S2][S3].
The Judiciary Committee held a hearing on February 3, 2016, but never voted the bill out of committee [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos victims and their families keep the status quo: their claim information stays out of public court dockets and defendant companies do not get the quarterly claim ledger the bill would have created. Companies facing asbestos lawsuits and their insurers lose the litigation tool they sought.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call ever occurred. The bill's sponsors and both cosponsors were Republicans [S3][S4], but the Senate never voted, so the party split on the merits was never tested.

industries.industry: Companies facing asbestos lawsuits (manufacturers, builders, and product sellers still defending exposure claims)
industries.note: The bill would have handed them a public, quarterly ledger of every claim and claimant at the asbestos trusts they face in court, plus on-request claim and payment data — ammunition for contesting, delaying, or shrinking payouts to sick workers and their families. Their gain would have come directly at those claimants' expense.
Insurers paying asbestos judgments would have received the same claim-level data through lawsuits, helping them dispute or reduce what they owe. The bill died before any of this took effect.

industries.industry: Asbestos bankruptcy trusts (524(g) trusts administering compensation funds)
industries.note: These trusts exist to pay people harmed by asbestos; the bill would have imposed quarterly public reporting on every individual claim and per-request data production at the trust's own cost, adding administrative burden and exposing claimants. The trusts' interest runs with the victims they pay.
